standard.title: Plot, character and setting
standard.description: discuss plot, character and setting, which are features of stories
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can recognise different types of literary texts and identify features including events and characters (AC9EFLE03). They have not yet discussed plot, character and setting as the three core structural features of stories, or explored how these features operate across different story types.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students discuss plot, character and setting as features of stories, recognising these across different story types including traditional tales and narratives.

nodes.label: Stories have characters
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify characters in stories and describe what kind of character they are — their qualities, roles and relationships.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the main character(s) in a story and describe at least two qualities or characteristics of one.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and describe characters across a range of story types, discussing character qualities, roles (protagonist, antagonist, helper), and how characters are similar or different across texts.
wider: Compare how the same character type (e.g. a trickster, a helper) appears in stories from different traditions
Discuss how animal characters in fables reflect human characteristics — what human qualities the author has given the animal and why
success_criteria: Student identifies the main character and describes at least two of their qualities
Student uses evidence from the text to support their description

nodes.label: Stories have a setting
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the setting of a story — where and when it takes place — and discuss whether it is realistic or imagined.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the setting of a given story (where and when) and state whether it seems realistic or imagined.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and describe settings across a range of texts, discussing time and place, whether settings are realistic or imagined, and how setting shapes the story's feel or events.
wider: Compare settings from stories set in the past, present and imagined worlds — discuss how setting shapes what is possible in the story
Explore how settings in Australian stories reflect Australian landscape and culture
success_criteria: Student describes the setting with reference to both place and time
Student states whether the setting is realistic or imagined and gives a reason

nodes.label: Stories have a plot
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the plot of a story — the sequence of events including a problem and how it is resolved.
nodes.minimum_width: Retell the main events of a story in order, identifying the problem and how it is resolved.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the plot of a story including the key events, the problem or challenge faced by characters, and the resolution, across a range of story types.
wider: Compare plots across two texts of the same story type (e.g. two traditional tales) and identify similarities in plot structure
Discuss what would happen to the plot if the setting or character were changed
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify the problem and resolution in a plot cannot engage with N4's analysis of how plot, character and setting interact — that integration depends on students having a functional concept of plot as a problem-resolution sequence.

response_modes.reason: Identifying 'the problem' in a story requires a reasoning move beyond sequencing — students need to judge which events constitute the complication versus background events. A scaffold ('What did the character want? What stopped them? How did it get fixed?') supports this.

success_criteria: Student retells main plot events in order
Student identifies the problem and resolution in the story

nodes.label: Plot, character and setting work together
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss how plot, character and setting work together as features of a story — how each influences the others.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how the setting or a character quality influences an event in the plot of a given story.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss how plot, character and setting interact in a story — how the setting shapes what events are possible, how character qualities drive plot events, and how these three elements together create the story.
wider: Identify similar characters and settings in different story types (traditional tales, narrative poems, fables) and discuss how the three features function across these forms
Explore how changing one element — e.g. moving a traditional tale to a different setting — would affect the other elements

response_modes.reason: Understanding plot, character and setting as a system — not three separate checklists — is the endpoint of this descriptor. Students need to see how these features depend on each other to form a coherent story.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Exploring what changes when one element is altered, or comparing how these features work across story types, gives advancing students genuine analytical leverage and opens rich creative-critical territory.
success_criteria: Student explains how at least one of plot, character or setting influences another element in a story
Student discusses all three features in relation to a given text
